title: Interface-Confined Superconductivity with Thickness-Independent Superfluid Stiffness in (Pb,Sn)Te/FeTe Bilayers
authors: Zi-Jie Yan, Hongtao Rong, Yiyuan Luo, Yufei Zhao, Pu Xiao, Zihao Wang, Lok-Kan Lai, Annie G. Wang, Zhiyuan Xi, Yanxing Li, Xiaoyu Wei, Ke Wang, Binghai Yan, Chih-Kang Shih, Cui-Zu Chang
abstract: Interface-induced superconductivity in FeTe-based heterostructures provides a promising route toward topological superconductivity, yet the roles of the neighboring layers topology, symmetry, and electronic structure remain unresolved. In this work, we employ molecular beam epitaxy to grow Pb1-xSnxTe/FeTe bilayers and use angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy to track the evolution of the Pb1-xSnxTe layer from a trivial insulator to a topological crystalline insulator hosting multiple Dirac surface states. Electrical transport measurements reveal robust superconductivity throughout the entire composition range, with a nearly constant superconducting transition temperature of ~12 K despite substantial changes in the electronic structure and topology of Pb1-xSnxTe. Double-coil mutual-inductance measurements further reveal comparable superfluid stiffness across the topological phase transition and nearly thickness-independent superfluid stiffness despite large variations in the constituent-layer thicknesses, demonstrating that superconductivity is confined near the interface. These results establish that superconductivity in FeTe-based heterostructures is largely insensitive to the topology, crystal symmetry, and detailed electronic structure of the neighboring layer, supporting a primary origin in modifications to the FeTe layer. The coexistence of interface-confined superconductivity and tunable multiple Dirac surface states in Pb1-xSnxTe/FeTe bilayers provides a versatile platform for exploring topological superconductivity and interactions among multiple Majorana zero modes.
summary: This work investigates superconductivity in $	ext{Pb}_{1-x}	ext{Sn}_x	ext{Te}/	ext{FeTe}$ bilayers, where the top layer undergoes a controlled topological phase transition. By measuring superconducting properties and superfluid stiffness, the authors conclude that the superconductivity is robustly confined to the interface region, suggesting its mechanism is intrinsic to the $	ext{FeTe}$ component rather than the topology of the adjacent material.
main_problem: The study investigates interface-induced superconductivity in $	ext{FeTe}$-based heterostructures, specifically addressing how the topology and electronic structure of neighboring layers influence this superconducting state.
main_result: Superconductivity is robust across a topological phase transition in the adjacent layer ($	ext{Pb}_{1-x}	ext{Sn}_x	ext{Te}$), suggesting that superconductivity originates primarily from modifications within the $	ext{FeTe}$ layer itself, confined near the interface.
method: The research combines experimental techniques like MBE growth, ARPES for electronic structure mapping, and double-coil mutual inductance measurements to probe superfluid stiffness. Theoretical calculations are used to model the topological transitions in the adjacent material.
model_or_system: The physical system is $	ext{Pb}_{1-x}	ext{Sn}_x	ext{Te}/	ext{FeTe}$ bilayers, where $x$ tunes the electronic structure of the top layer from a trivial insulator to a topological crystalline insulator (TCI). The analysis focuses on the interplay between this tunable topology and superconductivity.
key_observables: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), superfluid stiffness ($ho_s$), evolution of Dirac surface states, and band gap closing/reopening across the composition range.
important_parameters: Sn concentration ($x$) in $	ext{Pb}_{1-x}	ext{Sn}_x	ext{Te}$, which drives the topological phase transition; bilayer thickness (analyzed for saturation effects).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that superconductivity is interface-confined, suggesting its origin lies in the $	ext{FeTe}$ layer rather than being dictated by the bulk topology of the neighboring material.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate ARPES measurements showing Dirac cone emergence with $x$, and transport measurements demonstrating constant superfluid stiffness despite topological changes.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the physical system and methods, then uses ARPES to map the topological transition in $	ext{Pb}_{1-x}	ext{Sn}_x	ext{Te}$, followed by electrical/inductance measurements confirming robust superconductivity insensitive to this transition, leading to the conclusion of interface confinement.
why_interesting: While primarily condensed matter physics, the study involves engineered interfaces and superconducting phenomena that can be relevant to quantum computing platforms utilizing topological superconductors or Majorana zero modes at boundaries.
